conventional_commits.notes: Reinforced in P01-M03-L02. Applied 50/72 rule across 5 rewrite exercises. Correctly challenged capitalization-as-rule framing: CC spec uses lowercase descriptions and capitalization is a project-level style choice, not a spec requirement. Non-negotiables confirmed: imperative mood, 50-char target / 72-char hard cap, no trailing period, meaningful specificity. Previous: Complete understanding of type(scope): description structure, 11 commit types, breaking change syntax, and commit body judgment.

semantic_versioning.notes: NEW SKILL. Strong understanding of SemVer (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and how Conventional Commits drive automatic version bumps: feat → MINOR (1.2.0 → 1.3.0), fix → PATCH (1.2.0 → 1.2.1), feat! or BREAKING CHANGE → MAJOR (1.2.0 → 2.0.0). Understanding that tools like semantic-release read commit messages and automatically determine next version number. Recognition that commit messages become source of truth for versioning strategy. Understanding of backward compatibility implications: PATCH (bug fixes, safe to auto-update), MINOR (new features, backward compatible), MAJOR (breaking changes, review before updating).

commit_type_selection.notes: NEW SKILL. Exceptional pattern recognition for commit type selection based on intent rather than mechanics. Correctly distinguished: feat vs fix (user-facing impact, SemVer bump), refactor vs perf (motivation: organization/structure vs performance optimization), docs vs style (code functionality vs formatting), chore vs build (general maintenance vs build system changes). Understanding that same code change can have different types based on primary motivation (e.g., extracting queries for organization = refactor, extracting queries to reduce roundtrips = perf). Six months later, someone debugging uses type to determine investigation strategy. Demonstrated mature judgment: when multiple types apply, choose based on primary intent and user perspective.

imperative_mood_writing.notes: Reinforced in P01-M03-L02. Applied consistently across all 5 rewrite exercises without error. Used 'if applied' test correctly. Previous: perfect understanding of imperative mood for commit descriptions.

breaking_change_documentation.notes: NEW SKILL. Strong understanding of breaking change syntax and requirements. Breaking change defined as: any modification requiring user/developer action to maintain existing functionality (removing features, changing API signatures, modifying config formats, renaming env vars, changing default behavior, updating minimum dependencies). Two syntaxes understood: type(scope)! or BREAKING CHANGE: in commit body (both trigger MAJOR version bump). Understanding of what makes changes breaking vs non-breaking: changing config format/structure = breaking, changing config values = usually not breaking; adding optional features = not breaking, removing features = breaking; deprecating but not removing = not breaking (gives migration time). Real Helm examples generated for API endpoint changes, authentication config changes, and dependency version requirements.

commit_body_formatting.notes: NEW SKILL. Strong understanding of when and how to write commit bodies. When to include: complex 'why' reasoning, breaking changes, multiple related changes, implementation details (non-obvious), trade-offs/decisions explained. When to skip: header is self-explanatory, change is trivial, code diff is obvious. Formatting rules understood: 72-character line wrapping (terminals display 80, Git adds 8 indent = 72 for content), blank line separates header from body, multiple paragraphs allowed, bullet points for lists. Structure recommendations understood: technical changes section (what changed), user impact section (why care), test coverage (thoroughness), quantified improvements (numbers not adjectives). 'Would Future Me Understand?' test for deciding body inclusion.

git_footer_syntax.notes: NEW SKILL. Understanding of Git commit footer syntax for metadata and issue linking. Closes #N syntax for automatic issue closing when commit is merged. Footer separated from body by blank line. Multiple footers allowed (Closes #123, Co-authored-by: Name <email>). Understanding that GitHub parses footers for automation: Closes/Fixes/Resolves keywords close issues, Co-authored-by adds contributors to commit. Trailers format: Key: Value with colon separator. Common trailers: Reviewed-by, Tested-by, Signed-off-by, Acked-by. Footer used in all checkpoint 4 exercises showing proper issue linking.
